stem: The student wants to provide an example of a cleaner fish. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Cleaner fish are species that feed by removing parasites and dead skin from other fish.
• Larger reef fish often line up at "cleaning stations," fixed spots on a reef where cleaner fish gather.
• The bluestreak cleaner wrasse, a small striped fish of Indo-Pacific reefs, eats parasites off the bodies of other fish.
• One bluestreak cleaner wrasse may inspect more than 2,000 visiting fish in a single day.
choices: Cleaner fish are species that feed by picking parasites and dead skin off the bodies of other fish.
The bluestreak cleaner wrasse is a cleaner fish: it eats parasites off the bodies of other reef fish.
Larger reef fish often line up at cleaning stations, fixed reef spots where cleaner fish gather.
Every reef fish in the Indo-Pacific is a cleaner fish that removes parasites from other fish.
explanation: The goal asks for an example, so you need one named instance tied to the category. Choice B names a specific fish, the bluestreak cleaner wrasse, and links it to the category by saying it eats parasites off other fish.

A.why: You picked a general statement about cleaner fish as a group. It defines the category but never names a specific fish, so it gives no example. This is the wrong-level trap.

C.why: You went for a vivid detail about cleaning stations. It describes where cleaner fish gather but doesn't name any particular cleaner fish.

D.why: The notes never say every Indo-Pacific reef fish is a cleaner fish. The larger fish that line up at cleaning stations are the ones getting cleaned. This choice also makes a sweeping claim when the goal asked for one example.

stem: The student wants to make a generalization about body waves. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Body waves are seismic waves that travel through Earth's interior rather than along its surface.
• Primary (P) waves are body waves that squeeze and stretch rock as they pass through it.
• Secondary (S) waves are body waves that shake rock from side to side.
• After an earthquake, body waves generally reach distant seismometers before surface waves do.
choices: P waves squeeze and stretch rock as they pass, while S waves shake rock from side to side.
P waves are body waves that squeeze and stretch rock as they pass through Earth's interior.
Body waves, which travel through Earth's interior, generally reach seismometers before surface waves.
Surface waves, which travel along Earth's exterior, generally reach seismometers before body waves.
explanation: A generalization makes a claim about the whole category, with no single instance as its subject. Choice C makes body waves as a group its subject and states something true of them in general: they usually arrive before surface waves.

A.why: You picked a choice that compares two specific kinds of body wave. Contrasting P waves with S waves stays at the level of instances, so it isn't a claim about body waves as a whole. This is the subtype's main trap.

B.why: This choice is about one specific type, P waves, rather than body waves in general. It's an example, and the goal asked for a generalization.

D.why: This reverses the notes. Body waves reach seismometers before surface waves, not after.

stem: The student wants to present an example of a natural dye. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Natural dyes are colorants obtained from plants, animals, or minerals.
• Synthetic dyes, made from manufactured chemical compounds, spread widely after the 1850s.
• Madder is a plant whose roots yield a red colorant; cloth dyed with it has been found in ancient Egyptian tombs.
• Mauveine, a purple colorant discovered in 1856, was the first synthetic dye.
choices: Natural dyes are colorants obtained from plants, animals, or minerals rather than from manufactured compounds.
Madder, a plant whose roots yield a red colorant, is a natural dye used on cloth since ancient Egypt.
Mauveine, a purple colorant discovered in 1856, was the first dye made from manufactured compounds.
Natural dyes, used on cloth since ancient Egypt, were entirely replaced by synthetic dyes in 1856.
explanation: The goal asks for an example, so you need one named dye that belongs to the natural category. Choice B names madder, says the colorant comes from a plant (which the notes define as natural), and calls it a natural dye.

A.why: You picked a definition of the whole category. It explains what natural dyes are but names no particular dye, so it gives no example. This is the wrong-level trap.

C.why: Mauveine is a specific dye, but the notes call it synthetic. You found an example of the wrong category.

D.why: The notes say synthetic dyes spread after the 1850s, not that they fully replaced natural dyes in 1856. This choice also names no specific dye.

stem: The student wants to make a generalization about antibodies. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins produced by immune cells called B cells.
• Each antibody binds to one specific target molecule, known as its antigen.
• Immunoglobulin G (IgG) is the most abundant antibody in human blood.
• Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is found mainly in saliva, tears, and mucus.
choices: IgG is the most abundant antibody in human blood, whereas IgA is found mainly in saliva and tears.
Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins, made by B cells, that each bind to one specific antigen.
IgA is an antibody that is found mainly in saliva, tears, and mucus rather than in the blood.
Antibodies, including IgG, are found mainly in saliva, tears, and mucus rather than in blood.
explanation: A generalization is a claim about the whole category. Choice B makes antibodies in general its subject and states features true of all of them: their shape, where they come from, and how they bind.

A.why: You picked a choice that compares two specific antibodies. Setting IgG against IgA stays at the level of instances and says nothing about antibodies as a group. This is the subtype's main trap.

C.why: This choice is about one specific antibody, IgA. It gives an example, but the goal asked for a generalization.

D.why: The notes say IgG is the most abundant antibody in blood, and only IgA is found mainly in saliva, tears, and mucus. This choice applies IgA's location to all antibodies, IgG included.

stem: The student wants to provide an example of an artist who worked in an intaglio technique. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• In intaglio printmaking, lines are cut or etched into a metal plate, and ink is held in those sunken lines.
• Etching is an intaglio technique in which acid eats lines into a coated plate.
• In relief printmaking, such as woodcut, ink sits on the raised surface of a carved block.
• Dutch artist Rembrandt van Rijn produced roughly 300 etchings during the 1600s.
choices: In intaglio printmaking, lines are cut or etched into a metal plate, which then holds ink in them.
In woodcut, a relief technique, ink sits on the raised surface of a block carved by the artist.
Dutch artist Rembrandt van Rijn produced roughly 300 woodcuts, a relief technique, in the 1600s.
Dutch artist Rembrandt van Rijn produced roughly 300 etchings, an intaglio technique, in the 1600s.
explanation: The goal asks for a specific artist tied to intaglio. Rembrandt is the only artist in the notes, and Choice D links him to intaglio by naming his etchings as an intaglio technique. Notice the switch in terms: the note about Rembrandt says "etchings," not "intaglio," so you have to connect it to the note that says etching is an intaglio technique.

A.why: You picked a general description of intaglio. It explains the process but names no artist, so it gives no example. This is the wrong-level trap.

B.why: This choice describes woodcut, which the notes classify as relief, not intaglio. It also names no artist.

C.why: The notes say Rembrandt made etchings, not woodcuts. This choice misstates his medium and ties him to relief printmaking instead of intaglio.

stem: The student wants to make a generalization about legumes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Legumes are plants whose seeds grow in pods.
• Most legumes are rich sources of plant protein.
• Cooked lentils contain about 9 grams of protein per half cup.
• Cooked chickpeas contain about 7 grams of protein per half cup.
• Nutritionists often recommend legumes as an alternative to meat.
choices: Cooked lentils contain about 9 grams of protein per half cup, while chickpeas contain about 7 grams.
Most legumes, plants whose seeds grow in pods, are rich sources of plant protein.
Chickpeas, which grow in pods, contain about 7 grams of protein per half cup when cooked.
All legumes contain at least 7 grams of protein per half cup, as lentils and chickpeas do.
explanation: The goal asks for a generalization, so you want a claim about legumes as a whole category, with no single legume as the subject. Choice B uses the plural category noun with "most" and draws only on the category-level notes. It makes the broad claim the goal asks for.

A.why: You picked a sentence that compares two specific legumes. Putting lentils next to chickpeas is still a statement about individual instances, not about legumes in general.

C.why: You picked a single example. Chickpeas are one legume, and a fact about one instance isn't a generalization about the whole category.

D.why: This choice is worded as a generalization, but it stretches two examples into a rule about "all legumes." The notes say only that "most" legumes are rich in protein and never give a minimum for the whole group.

stem: The student wants to provide an example of an equal-area projection. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A map projection is a method of representing Earth's curved surface on a flat plane.
• Equal-area projections preserve the relative sizes of regions.
• The Mercator projection, developed in 1569, preserves shapes and directions but enlarges regions near the poles.
• The Gall-Peters projection shows every region at its correct relative size.
choices: Equal-area projections are map projections that preserve the relative sizes of the regions they show.
The Mercator projection, developed in 1569, is a projection that preserves shapes and directions.
The Mercator projection is an equal-area projection, though it enlarges regions near the poles.
The Gall-Peters projection, which shows every region at its correct relative size, is an equal-area projection.
explanation: An example has to name one specific projection and connect it to the property in the goal. The note on Gall-Peters never says "equal-area." It says "correct relative size," and that is exactly what the definition note says equal-area projections preserve. Choice D names Gall-Peters and labels it equal-area, so it does what the goal asks.

A.why: You picked a definition of the category. No specific projection is named, so this defines what an equal-area projection is without giving an example of one.

B.why: This names a specific projection, but it ties that projection to the wrong property. Preserving shapes and directions isn't what the goal asks about.

C.why: A projection that enlarges polar regions doesn't preserve relative size, so the notes rule out calling Mercator equal-area. This choice contradicts its own second half.

stem: The student wants to make a generalization about resist-dyeing techniques. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Resist dyeing is a family of textile techniques used to create patterns.
• In resist dyeing, parts of a fabric are protected so that dye cannot reach them.
• The protected areas usually keep the fabric's original color.
• Batik, practiced in Java, uses wax to block dye.
• Shibori, practiced in Japan, uses binding, stitching, or folding.
choices: In resist-dyeing techniques, parts of a fabric are protected from dye, usually leaving patterns in its original color.
Batik, a technique practiced in Java, uses wax to keep dye from reaching certain parts of a fabric.
Whereas batik artisans in Java use wax to block dye, shibori artisans in Japan use binding, stitching, or folding.
Every resist-dyeing technique relies on wax to block dye, as the batik artisans of Java do.
explanation: A generalization is a claim about the whole family of techniques. Choice A takes "resist-dyeing techniques" as its subject and states what they have in common: protected areas that usually keep the original color. No single technique is the focus.

B.why: You picked one instance. Batik is a single technique, so a sentence about it gives an example rather than a generalization about the category.

C.why: You picked a contrast between two specific techniques. Comparing batik and shibori is a comparison, not a claim about resist dyeing as a whole.

D.why: This turns one technique's method into a rule for the whole category. The notes show that shibori uses no wax, so "every" goes beyond what the notes support.

stem: The student wants to provide an example of a confined aquifer. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• An aquifer is an underground layer of rock or sediment that holds water.
• A confined aquifer is sealed above and below by layers that water cannot easily pass through.
• The Ogallala Aquifer, beneath eight U.S. states, is largely open to water seeping down from the surface.
• The Dakota Aquifer in South Dakota lies between impermeable layers of shale.
choices: A confined aquifer is an underground water layer sealed by layers that water cannot easily pass through.
The Ogallala Aquifer, which lies beneath eight U.S. states, is an example of a confined aquifer.
The Dakota Aquifer, which lies between impermeable layers of shale, is a confined aquifer.
The Ogallala Aquifer, extending beneath eight U.S. states, is larger than the Dakota Aquifer.
explanation: An example must name one specific aquifer and connect it to the property in the goal. "Impermeable" means that water cannot easily pass through, so shale above and below makes the Dakota Aquifer fit the definition of a confined aquifer. Choice C names it and gives it that label.

A.why: You picked the definition. It says what a confined aquifer is, but it never names one, so there is no example.

B.why: The notes say the Ogallala is open to water seeping down from the surface, which means it isn't sealed above. Calling it confined reverses what the notes say.

D.why: The notes never give the Dakota Aquifer's size, so this comparison isn't supported. It also says nothing about which aquifer is confined.

stem: The student wants to make a generalization about keystone species. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• A keystone species has an effect on its ecosystem that is large relative to its numbers.
• Removing a keystone species typically causes major changes throughout its ecosystem.
• In Yellowstone, gray wolves limit elk grazing along rivers.
• On Pacific coasts, sea otters eat sea urchins, which would otherwise destroy kelp forests.
choices: In Yellowstone, gray wolves are a keystone species that limits how much elk graze along rivers.
Keystone species affect their ecosystems out of proportion to their numbers, and their removal typically causes major changes.
Both gray wolves and sea otters are keystone species that protect the plants of their ecosystems.
Keystone species are always predators, such as the gray wolves of Yellowstone and Pacific sea otters.
explanation: The goal asks for a generalization, so the subject should be keystone species as a group. Choice B uses the plural category noun and states what holds for the category, drawing only on the two category-level notes. Neither wolves nor otters is its subject.

A.why: You picked one instance. A sentence about Yellowstone's wolves is an example of a keystone species, not a claim about keystone species in general.

C.why: You picked a pairing of two specific animals. Pointing out what wolves and otters share still keeps you at the level of instances, not the whole category.

D.why: This is worded as a generalization, but it turns two predator examples into a rule with "always." Nothing in the notes says every keystone species is a predator.
